Expectation1: Maintain regular communication with family members
Situation1: A family member has a new job and has shared some initial excitement about it with their relatives.
Situation2: Many prospects ask detailed technical questions about the new service that the script only partially addresses.
Story: I stared at my phone, thumb hovering over the call button. My daughter had just texted about her new job, her excitement practically leaping off the screen. She wanted to talk, to share every detail, and I knew how much it meant to her that I listened and celebrated with her. But my shift as a telemarketer had just started, and the call queue was already filling up. My supervisor expected me to handle every customer objection with patience, to answer technical questions about our new service—even though the script barely scratched the surface. Yesterday, a prospect grew frustrated when I couldn’t explain a feature, and I’d felt the sting of disappointment from my manager. Now, as I weighed the phone in my hand, I felt torn. My family needed me to be present, to show I cared. My job needed me to be focused, to keep up with the relentless pace and demands. The pressure built inside me, a tug-of-war between being the grandparent my family expected and the employee my boss demanded. I closed my eyes, heart pounding, caught between two worlds that both needed me right now.
